question: Delamination claims are up - what's going on?

guard_decision.reason: The question asks to investigate why delamination_claim_rate has increased. This is a classic investigative query that defaults to examining the most recent data across available dimensions (batch, press_line, month) to surface patterns. The ontology provides delamination_claim_rate as a metric and sufficient object/link relationships to explore potential root causes (production batches, press lines, quality inspections, veneer yields).

metrics.name: delamination_claim_rate
metrics.definition: Warranty claims with defect_type "delamination" per 100 decks, counted only among decks that have reached 90 days of field maturity (90 days since ship_date as of the metric's as-of date). Decks younger than 90 days are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator.

metrics.name: first_pass_yield
metrics.definition: The share of decks in a production batch that pass quality inspection on the first inspection, with no rework or reprocessing. Computed as decks passing first inspection divided by total decks inspected in the batch.

metrics.name: on_time_ship_rate
metrics.definition: The share of orders shipped on or before their committed ship date (order_date plus standard lead time), out of all orders with a non-cancelled status.

metrics.name: scrap_cost_per_batch
metrics.definition: Total material and labor cost attributed to decks scrapped during production for a batch, divided by the batch's planned deck count. Scrap is any deck that fails inspection and is not reworked.

metrics.name: veneer_yield
metrics.definition: The fraction of a maple veneer material lot's received quantity that is actually drawn into production batches, versus left unused as remainder or trim. Computed as the sum of quantity_used across every batch that consumes the lot, divided by the lot's received quantity.

result.definition: Warranty claims with defect_type "delamination" per 100 decks, counted only among decks that have reached 90 days of field maturity (90 days since ship_date as of the metric's as-of date). Decks younger than 90 days are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator.
result.rationale: Delamination is a defect that surfaces with use, not at the moment of sale — a deck typically has to be ridden, get wet, and take a few impacts before a sub-par adhesive bond starts to show itself. A metric of raw claims over decks shipped is biased toward whichever batches are oldest, because they have had the most time to accumulate claims, and it is biased against the newest batches, which look artificially safe simply because they have not been skated long enough to start to fail. That makes "raw claims over shipped" actively misleading during exactly the window when catching a bad batch matters most: a newly-discovered material problem would look clean under that definition for months, by which time far more decks have shipped. Matching on maturity — comparing batches only once each has had the same amount of field time — is what makes the batches comparable at all, and it is the difference between "we have a lot problem" and "we have a plausible pattern that might just be an aging artifact."

result.definition: The fraction of a maple veneer material lot's received quantity that is actually drawn into production batches, versus left unused as remainder or trim. Computed as the sum of quantity_used across every batch that consumes the lot, divided by the lot's received quantity.
result.rationale: Veneer is the highest-variance input cost and the most common root cause of delamination. Tracking yield at the lot grain (not the supplier average) is what makes a single bad lot detectable instead of being diluted into a supplier's otherwise-normal track record.

result.definition: The share of decks in a production batch that pass quality inspection on the first inspection, with no rework or reprocessing. Computed as decks passing first inspection divided by total decks inspected in the batch.
result.rationale: First-pass yield is the earliest signal of a process or material problem, before it becomes a warranty claim months later. It is scoped to the first inspection specifically because counting yield after rework hides the cost of the rework itself and would make a struggling line look identical to a clean one.

final_answer:
## What's going on

Using **delamination_claim_rate** ("warranty claims with defect_type 'delamination' per 100 decks, counted only among decks that have reached 90 days of field maturity"), the vast majority of ~280 production batches sit at 0, with a normal-noise band up to ~9%. Three batches are clearly separated from that pack:

| Batch | Delamination claim rate |
|---|---|
| **B0050** | 19.35 (highest fleet-wide) |
| **B0203** | 12.00 (2nd highest) |
| **B0233** | 10.34 (3rd highest) |

I anchored on B0050 (the single most extreme reading) and traversed its `consumes` link to its five input material lots. One of them — **LOT-MAP-011**, a maple veneer lot from **SUP01** — also turns up in B0203 and B0233's input lists. I then checked roughly 20 other batches spanning the full range of claim rates (including 8 batches with a 0% delamination rate and several other elevated batches like B0049, B0030, B0126, B0069, B0157, B0011, B0181, etc.) — LOT-MAP-011 appeared in *none* of them. So every known occurrence of this lot lines up exactly with the three worst-performing batches in the dataset, and it's absent from every clean batch I sampled.

I also ruled out a couple of false leads: an epoxy-resin lot (LOT-EPO-012) initially looked suspicious because it appeared in several elevated batches, but it also showed up in multiple zero-rate batches — it's just a heavily-used, generic lot, not a real signal. Same story for a recurring grip-tape lot. LOT-MAP-011 is the one candidate that cleanly separates high-delamination batches from clean ones.

First-pass yield for B0050, B0203, and B0233 was normal-to-high (0.91–1.00) — expected, since delamination is a field-maturity defect (per the metric's own rationale) that wouldn't show up at initial inspection, so this doesn't contradict the finding.

**This is a correlational finding**, not a proven causal link — I don't have a controlled comparison, just an unusually strong co-occurrence between one specific veneer lot and the three worst delamination readings in the fleet.

**Action taken:** I've submitted `quarantine_batch` proposals for B0050, B0203, and B0233 (all `pending_approval` — a human still needs to approve each before it affects any tool's view of the data). I did not propose a broader SUP01 supplier-level action, since two other SUP01 veneer lots (LOT-MAP-001, LOT-MAP-010) appear in several zero-rate batches and don't show the same pattern — the evidence implicates this specific lot, not the supplier as a whole.
